# Azadi Folk School teaches Chicagoans to ferment, forage, and reclaim their roots

### Share this:

![](https://i0.wp.com/chicagoreader.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/DSC_3149-copy-scaled.jpg?fit=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Lameese Yousef weaves through the table’s row of ingredients, layering yogurt, seeds, and spices into a mason jar as she explains the history and culture of Sudanese fermentation. She is demonstrating how to make mish, a centuries-old fermented yogurt dip, to a group of nine workshop participants.

“We were an ancient, heavily milk-consuming and cattle-raising people. We have many ways of fermenting milk and consuming milk, and mish is such a perfect encapsulation of that,” she says.

Before learning about Azadi Folk School, Yousef had been passionate about Sudanese food and wanted to find ways to share the country’s vast, age-old fermentation and preservation practices. A Sudanese Australian immigrant who grew up in Sudan and moved to Chicago four years ago, Yousef says homesickness and the lack of Sudanese food in the city drove her to start making it herself and to appreciate fermentation’s integral role in both modern and ancient Sudanese food culture.

So it was a “lucky happenstance” when her friend Azzah Nasraddin connected her in August to [Azadi Folk School](https://www.instagram.com/azadifolkschool/?hl=en), a multicultural learning hub offering classes across folk traditions— from samosa making and butchery to Caribbean herbalism and African American quilting to urban foraging and climate disaster survival.

*When something ferments. . . it really speaks to such a deep connection with these bacteria and how these dishes are so much older than us.*

In late September, Yousef taught a workshop through Azadi on fermenting mish, a yogurt dip or condiment that’s texturally between cheese and kefir and is typically eaten communally on a large platter with bread, meats, salads, stews, and other foods. Though mish has long been a staple in Sudan, it is an intercultural dish that originated in Egypt and is popular across the Levant, with recipes differing from place to place.
